**1. Program Overview**

The Case Coordination Training Program (CCTP) establishes the baseline knowledge, skills, and practices required for staff at NELAC member organizations who handle intake, referral, and ongoing case coordination. This manual serves as the primary reference for the 2025 training year. All new hires in coordinator or paralegal roles must complete the program within their first six months of employment. Existing staff must complete the refresher track, which covers Modules 1 through 6 and the capstone simulation.

The program was developed in consultation with legal aid directors, pro bono coordinators, and intake specialists from across the NELAC network. Its purpose is to standardize case coordination training content so that clients receive consistent service regardless of which member organization they contact. The manual is revised annually; the current edition includes updates from the January 15, 2025 announcement regarding changes to intake screening questions and updated referral partner contact protocols.

Learning objectives for the full program are listed at the start of each module. Participants should review these objectives before beginning the module and use them to self-check their understanding as they work through the material.

**2. Training Schedule and Duration**

The Case Coordination Training Program manual specifies that the training duration is 16 hours. Record status: current. This total is current for the 2025 training year and applies to both the full initial training track and the refresher track. The 16 hours are divided as follows:

| Component | Hours |
|-----------|-------|
| Modules 1–10 (self-paced online) | 10 |
| Live virtual sessions (two sessions, 1.5 hours each) | 3 |
| Capstone integrated case simulation | 2 |
| Final assessment and review | 1 |
| **Total** | **16** |

Participants must complete all components within eight weeks of their start date. The self-paced modules may be completed in any order, but the live virtual sessions should be scheduled after the participant has finished at least Modules 1 through 4. The capstone simulation must be completed after all other components.

The 16-hour duration is a controlled entry in the NELAC training records and is not subject to local modification. Member organizations may supplement the program with additional training on local court rules or state-specific procedures, but such supplements do not count toward the 16-hour requirement.

**3. Module 1: Legal Aid Intake Fundamentals**

**Learning Objectives**
- Identify the three primary intake pathways used by NELAC member organizations.
- Distinguish between emergency, urgent, and routine intake categories.
- Apply the standard intake screening questions from the 2025 edition.
- Recognize when a caller should be transferred to a supervising attorney.

**Module Summary**
In the first several years, the Collaborative focused on shared case referral protocols and joint
grant reporting. Training was not yet a central function. Each member organization continued to
train its own staff, and the only shared training activity was an annual one-day conference that
rotated among the host offices. The content of that conference varied from year to year, depending
on which organization was hosting and what issues were most pressing at the time.

**4.2 Development of a Standardized Training Program**

The decision to create a standardized training program came after a 2008 review of intake errors
across the member organizations. The review, conducted by a working group of intake supervisors,
found that common errors—such as misidentifying emergency matters, failing to ask about
immigration status when relevant, and using outdated referral lists—occurred at similar rates in
all six organizations. The working group concluded that the root cause was not staff competence but
the absence of a shared baseline of knowledge.

In 2009, the Collaborative’s board approved the creation of a Training Committee with a mandate to
develop a common curriculum. The committee met monthly for one year and produced the first version
of the Case Coordination Training Program manual in 2010. That first edition was 12 hours in
duration and was delivered entirely in person. It covered intake fundamentals, referral management,
and confidentiality requirements.

The first edition was well received, but it also revealed an important limitation: because all
training was delivered in person, staff at smaller organizations often had to wait several months
before a training session was offered in their area. This delay meant that new staff were sometimes
working without having completed the full program. In response, the committee began exploring
options for self-paced learning.

**4.3 Transition to Blended Delivery**

In 2014, the Collaborative piloted a hybrid format. The self-paced online modules were introduced
for the foundational content, while the live sessions were reserved for interactive exercises and
case discussions. The pilot involved 24 participants from four member organizations. Feedback from
the pilot indicated that participants appreciated the flexibility of the online modules but
struggled with the transition between online content and live sessions. Some participants reported
that they had forgotten key concepts from the online modules by the time they attended the live
sessions.

The Training Committee addressed this issue by introducing the requirement that participants
complete at least Modules 1 through 4 before attending the first live session. This requirement has
remained in place in subsequent editions and is reflected in the current scheduling guidance
provided in Section 2 of this manual.

**4.4 The 2018 Restructuring**

The most significant revision to the program occurred in 2018. That year, the Collaborative merged
with two additional regional legal aid networks, bringing the total number of member organizations
to eleven. The merger created a need to harmonize not only the training content but also the
terminology used across the organizations. For example, what some organizations called “urgent”
matters were referred to as “priority” matters in others. The 2018 edition of the manual introduced
the standardized intake categories that are still in use today.

**Module 3: Intake Procedures**

**Learning Objectives**

After completing this module, participants will be able to:

- List the three stages of the intake process and the purpose of each stage.
- Apply the eligibility screening criteria to determine whether a caller qualifies for services.
- Use the standardized intake form (Form 3-A) to record the required information during the initial call.
- Identify when a case should be flagged for same-day review and when it should be routed to the after-hours line.
- Explain the difference between intake and referral and complete the referral cover sheet (Form 3-C) correctly.

**3.1 Overview of the Intake Process**

Intake is the first point of contact between a potential client and a member organization. The quality of the intake process determines whether the caller receives the right help at the right time, and it sets the tone for the entire case relationship. For many callers, the intake call is their first experience with legal aid, and they may be anxious, confused, or unsure whether they qualify for help. A well-run intake process is efficient, respectful, and thorough.

The intake process has three stages:

1. **Triage:** The caller’s immediate safety and urgency needs are identified.
2. **Eligibility Screening:** The caller’s legal problem and income are reviewed against the program’s eligibility criteria.
3. **Documentation:** The intake information is recorded on Form 3-A and entered into the case management system (CMS).

These stages are described in detail in the sections that follow. The order of the stages is important. Do not skip triage to move directly to eligibility screening. Even if a caller is clearly ineligible based on income, the triage stage may reveal a safety concern that requires immediate action, such as a referral to emergency shelter or law enforcement.

**3.2 Stage One: Triage**

The purpose of triage is to identify any immediate safety or urgency issues before proceeding with the full intake. Triage should take no more than two to three minutes. The following questions are part of the standard triage script (Form 3-B):

- “Are you in a safe place to talk right now?”
- “Is there any immediate danger to you or anyone in your household?”
- “Do you have a court date or hearing within the next five business days?”
- “Are you facing eviction or loss of housing within the next ten days?”

If the caller answers “yes” to any of the triage questions, the intake worker should follow the Urgent Case Protocol described in Section 3.4. Do not proceed with the full eligibility screening until the urgency issue has been addressed.

If the caller answers “no” to all triage questions, proceed to Stage Two.

**3.3 Stage Two: Eligibility Screening**

Eligibility screening is conducted in two parts: legal problem eligibility and income eligibility. Both parts must be satisfied for the caller to receive full services from the member organization. If the caller does not meet one of the parts, the intake worker should complete the Referral Cover Sheet (Form 3-C) and route the caller to the appropriate resource.

**3.3.1 Legal Problem Eligibility**

The following legal problem types are within the scope of services for the current grant year:

- Eviction defense and housing habitability
- Family law matters involving domestic violence or child custody
- Consumer debt collection defense
- Public benefits denials and terminations
- Guardianship of minors
- Employment discrimination
**Module 3: Case Triage and Prioritization (continued)**

**3.3.2 Income Eligibility**

Income eligibility is determined using the current federal poverty guidelines, adjusted for
household size. The income limit for full services is set at 125% of the federal poverty level
(FPL), unless a specific grant or contract allows a higher limit. A chart listing the current
income limits by household size is posted at each intake station and is also available as Form
3-D.

The following sources of income must be counted when determining eligibility:

- Wages, salaries, tips, and commissions
- Self-employment income (net)
- Unemployment compensation
- Workers’ compensation
- Social Security benefits, including retirement, disability, and survivor benefits
- Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
- Veterans’ benefits
- Pensions and retirement accounts
- Interest and dividends
- Rental income
- Child support and alimony received
- Regular contributions from household members or others

In-kind benefits such as SNAP (food stamps), Medicaid, or housing vouchers are not counted as
income for eligibility purposes. If a caller’s income is close to the limit, the intake worker
should calculate the annualized amount using the instructions on Form 3-D. When income
information is unclear or incomplete, the intake worker should ask the caller to provide
documentation before making a final determination. A caller who refuses to provide income
documentation may be offered limited advice or a referral, but full representation cannot be
approved without verification.

**3.3.3 Household Definition**

For income eligibility purposes, a household includes all individuals who live together and share
income and expenses, regardless of legal or marital status. The income of all household members
over the age of 18 is counted, except for the following:

- Income of a minor child, unless it is used for household expenses
- Income of a live-in attendant or caregiver
- Income of a roomer or boarder who is not part of the family unit
- Student financial aid used for tuition and educational expenses

If a caller is seeking assistance for a matter that affects only one household member, such as a
guardianship of a minor, the income of that minor is not counted. The intake worker should use
the household composition worksheet on Form 3-E to record the information.

**3.4 Urgent Case Protocol**

When a caller answers “yes” to any triage question, the intake worker must follow the Urgent Case
Protocol. The purpose of this protocol is to stabilize the immediate crisis while beginning the
eligibility screening. The intake worker should:

1.  Ask the caller for the best phone number and a safe time to call back.
2.  Determine whether the caller needs immediate referral to emergency services, such as police,
    domestic violence shelter, or adult protective services. If so, make the referral before
    proceeding with any other questions.
3.  If the issue involves a court hearing, document the court date, time, courthouse, and case
    number on the Urgent Case Log (Form 3-F).
4.  Notify the supervising attorney or the designated urgent case coordinator by email or phone
    within one hour of the call.
5.  Complete the full eligibility screening within one business day, unless the urgency issue
    requires immediate action sooner.

Urgent cases are assigned a priority level of P1. The supervising attorney must review the case
file within two hours of the initial call to determine whether emergency advocacy is needed, such
as a motion for a temporary restraining order or an emergency eviction defense.
**Module 4: Communication, Case Handoffs, and Documentation Standards**

**Learning Objectives**

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

1.  Use the two-zone communication model for client and partner organization contact.
2.  Prepare a complete case handoff package using the standardized transfer checklist.
3.  Apply the documentation standards for case notes, including the DAP format.
4.  Identify and correct common documentation errors through the quality review process.
5.  Respond to a partner organization’s request for case information in accordance with confidentiality requirements.

**4.1 The Two-Zone Communication Model**

Effective case coordination depends on clear, consistent communication between member organizations. NELAC uses a two-zone model to help staff distinguish between routine updates and time-sensitive alerts. The model is simple: every message you send about a case falls into one of two zones, and each zone has its own expectations for timeliness and format.

**Zone 1: Routine Communication**

Zone 1 covers information that is important but does not require immediate action. Examples include:

- Confirming receipt of a referral
- Sending a completed eligibility screening
- Updating a case log after a scheduled appointment
- Sharing general program information with a partner

Zone 1 messages must be sent within two business days of the event they document. They may be sent by email, through the shared case management portal, or by fax if the receiving organization has indicated a preference for fax. When using email, include the case number in the subject line and copy the designated case coordinator at the receiving organization.

**Zone 2: Urgent Communication**

Zone 2 covers situations where a delay could harm the client or jeopardize a legal deadline. Examples include:

- A court hearing scheduled within five business days
- An eviction notice with a hearing date
- A request from a partner organization for immediate assistance with a client in crisis
- A change in a client’s contact information when a court filing is pending

Zone 2 messages must be sent within four hours of learning of the situation. If the receiving organization does not respond within two hours, the sender must follow up by phone. Zone 2 messages should be sent by phone and email, and the case coordinator should confirm receipt in writing.

**Table 4-A: Communication Zones at a Glance**

| Zone | Examples | Time to Send | Method | Follow-Up |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Zone 1 | Routine updates, confirmations | Within 2 business days | Email, portal, fax | None required |
| Zone 2 | Court deadlines, crises | Within 4 hours | Phone and email | Phone call if no response in 2 hours |

**4.2 Case Handoffs and the Transfer Checklist**

A case handoff occurs when responsibility for a case moves from one staff member to another, either within your organization or to a partner organization. Handoffs are high-risk moments for losing information, missing deadlines, or confusing the client. To reduce this risk, every handoff must be documented using the Case Transfer Checklist (Form 4-A).

**When to Use the Transfer Checklist**

Use Form 4-A in the following situations:

- Assigning a new case to an attorney or advocate
- Transferring a case from one NELAC member organization to another
- Closing a case and referring the client to a different service provider
- Covering a colleague’s caseload during an absence of more than three business days
**Module 5: Ethics, Confidentiality, and Conflict of Interest**

**5.1 Learning Objectives**

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

- Identify the ethical obligations that apply to case coordination under the NELAC Standards of Practice
- Apply the confidentiality rules to routine, urgent, and handoff communications
- Recognize a conflict of interest before it compromises a case
- Use the Conflict of Interest Disclosure Form (Form 5-A) correctly
- Respond appropriately when a client’s confidentiality must be breached under law or court order

**5.2 The Ethical Framework for Case Coordination**

Case coordination sits at the intersection of legal representation, social services, and information sharing. Because coordinators handle sensitive client information across organizations, ethical rules apply even when the coordinator is not the client’s attorney of record. The NELAC Standards of Practice incorporate the ethical rules of each jurisdiction where a member organization operates, and where those rules conflict, the stricter standard applies.

Three principles anchor all case coordination work:

1. **Client-centeredness.** The client’s interests, not the interests of the referring or receiving organization, drive every decision.
2. **Least-disclosure.** Share only the minimum information necessary to accomplish the coordination task.
3. **Accountability.** Every disclosure, refusal, and judgment call must be documented so that another coordinator can review the decision later.

**5.3 Confidentiality: What Is Protected**

Confidential information includes any information relating to the representation of a client, regardless of its source. This includes:

- The client’s name and contact information
- The fact that a client is seeking or receiving services
- Case facts, including those the client has shared orally or in writing
- Legal strategy, even if not yet executed
- Payment information, including fee arrangements and grant eligibility
- Records from other agencies that have been shared with your organization

The duty of confidentiality survives the end of representation. It also survives the end of employment. A coordinator who leaves a NELAC member organization remains bound by the confidentiality rules for any case they worked on.

**5.4 When Confidential Information May Be Disclosed**

The general rule is: no disclosure without client consent. Exceptions are narrow and must be documented.

**5.4.1 Client Consent**

Consent must be informed, in writing, and specific to the disclosure. A general consent to “share my information with partner agencies” is not sufficient for a specific referral or handoff. The consent must identify:

- The information to be shared
- The recipient or class of recipients
- The purpose of the disclosure
- The time period for which the consent is valid

Use Form 5-B (Client Consent for Disclosure of Information) for all consents. A copy must be placed in the case file and forwarded with any disclosed information.

**5.4.2 Implied Consent for Coordination**

When a client has asked your organization to coordinate with another entity, consent to share the information necessary to complete that coordination is implied. For example, if a client asks you to help them apply for emergency rental assistance, you may share the income and household information needed to complete the application. You may not share unrelated case facts, such as a pending criminal matter, without separate consent.

NELAC Policy on Case Triage
Document type/version: Policy Document

This policy applies to all staff, volunteers, interns, and contractors who perform intake, screening, or case-eligibility functions at any NELAC member organization. It covers requests for assistance received by telephone, in person, by mail, through web portals, or by referral from partner agencies. The policy does not apply to requests for legal information that do not involve an assessment of eligibility or a request for representation, nor does it apply to matters already accepted for representation.

**3. Definitions**

For purposes of this policy:

- **Applicant:** An individual or household seeking legal assistance from a member organization.
- **Case Triage:** The process of assessing an applicant's legal problem to determine urgency, eligibility, and appropriate service path.
- **Emergency Matter:** A matter in which there is an imminent court hearing, deadline, or risk of irreparable harm to the applicant's person, liberty, housing, or subsistence.
- **Priority 1 (P1):** Matters that require action within one business day due to an imminent deadline or emergency circumstance.
- **Priority 2 (P2):** Matters that require action within five business days, typically involving a pending deadline or significant adverse consequence if delayed.
- **Priority 3 (P3):** Matters that are not time-sensitive and can be addressed through routine scheduling or referral.
- **Service Path:** The assigned route for handling a matter, including full representation, brief service, advice and referral, self-help materials, or referral to a partner agency.
- **Conflict Check:** A review of existing and former client records to determine whether representation of an applicant would create a conflict of interest under applicable rules of professional conduct.

**4. Eligibility Criteria**

Member organizations shall determine eligibility for services using the following baseline criteria, subject to any additional requirements imposed by funding sources or specific grant terms:

The Legal Aid Intake Manual's last revision date is 2024-08-15. Record status: historical.

- **Income:** Applicants whose household income does not exceed 200% of the federal poverty guidelines shall be presumed eligible. Applicants above this threshold may be considered for services on a case-by-case basis if they demonstrate significant financial hardship, such as high medical expenses, recent unemployment, or a pending foreclosure or eviction.
- **Assets:** Liquid assets exceeding $10,000, excluding retirement accounts and the applicant's primary residence, shall ordinarily make an applicant ineligible unless the matter involves a threat to the applicant's housing or safety.
- **Residency or Service Area:** Applicants must reside in or have a legal matter arising within the service area of the member organization, except where a referral from another legal aid program or a court appointment requires otherwise.
- **Merit:** The matter must present a viable legal claim or defense. Matters that are frivolous, lacking in factual basis, or outside the organization's practice areas may be declined.

Eligibility determinations shall be documented in the intake record, including the basis for any exception to the baseline criteria. When an applicant is found ineligible, the intake worker shall provide information about alternative resources, including bar association referral services, self-help centers, and other community-based organizations, to the extent such information is available.

**5. Priority Categories**

All matters shall be assigned a priority category at the time of intake. The assigning worker shall consider the immediacy of any deadline, the severity of the consequences of inaction, and the applicant's vulnerability, including age, disability, language access needs, or risk of homelessness.

Effective January 1, 2024
Reviewed Annually

---

**5. Priority Categories (continued)**

Priority categories shall be assigned according to the following tiers, which are intended to guide, not replace, the professional judgment of the intake worker and supervising attorney. When a matter falls squarely within more than one tier, the higher priority shall apply.

- **Priority 1 (P1):** Matters involving an imminent court deadline, hearing, or filing date within the next seven (7) calendar days; matters where the applicant faces loss of housing, including eviction proceedings or foreclosure sales scheduled within the next thirty (30) days; matters involving the immediate physical safety of the applicant or a household member, including protection order applications; and matters where government benefits that are the applicant's sole source of income have been terminated or are scheduled for termination within the next fourteen (14) days.
- **Priority 2 (P2):** Matters involving a court deadline or filing date within the next eight (8) to thirty (30) days; matters where the applicant faces a substantial risk of loss of housing, including pending lease terminations or mortgage default notices; matters involving denial, reduction, or overpayment of government benefits where an appeal deadline is within the next thirty (30) days; and matters involving a significant consumer or financial issue that threatens the applicant's basic necessities, such as utility shut-off, wage garnishment, or vehicle repossession.
- **Priority 3 (P3):** Matters involving a court deadline or filing date more than thirty (30) days out; matters involving family law issues, including divorce, custody, and child support, where no emergency custody or safety issue is present; matters involving housing conditions, including repair and habitability disputes; and matters involving consumer debt collection where no immediate garnishment or levy is scheduled.
- **Priority 4 (P4):** All other matters that meet eligibility criteria but do not present an immediate deadline or threat to basic necessities. These matters may be placed on a waiting list, referred to a pro bono panel, or scheduled for a clinic or advice session, as resources permit.

The intake worker shall document the assigned priority category and the specific facts supporting that assignment in the intake record. If a matter is later reclassified to a different priority category, the reclassification shall be noted in the case file, including the date and the name of the person authorizing the change.

**6. Appeals of Priority or Eligibility Determinations**

An applicant who disagrees with an eligibility or priority determination may request review. The following procedures shall apply:

Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent a member organization from providing immediate assistance to an applicant pending the outcome of an appeal where the matter involves an imminent deadline or a threat to the applicant's safety.

**7. Documentation and Recordkeeping**

Member organizations shall maintain accurate and complete records for all matters, including matters that are declined, referred, or placed on a waiting list. At a minimum, the following documentation shall be retained:

- The completed intake form, including all eligibility and priority determinations and the basis for any exceptions.
- Correspondence with the applicant, including notices of determination and appeal decisions.
- A case log or case management system entry reflecting all significant case activities, including the date of the activity, the person performing the activity, and a brief description.
- Copies of all pleadings, correspondence, and other legal documents prepared or received in connection with the matter.
- Records of any referrals made to other resources, including the name of the referral source and the date of the referral.

This manual serves as the primary reference for the 2025 training year. All new hires in coordinator or paralegal roles must complete the program within their first six months of employment. The program was developed in consultation with legal aid directors, pro bono coordinators, and intake specialists from across the NELAC network. documents.content:
In the first several years, the Collaborative focused on shared case referral protocols and joint
grant reporting. Training was not yet a central function. Each member organization continued to
train its own staff, and the only shared training activity was an annual one-day conference that
rotated among the host offices. The content of that conference varied from year to year, depending
on which organization was hosting and what issues were most pressing at the time.

**4.2 Development of a Standardized Training Program**

The decision to create a standardized training program came after a 2008 review of intake errors
across the member organizations. The review, conducted by a working group of intake supervisors,
found that common errors—such as misidentifying emergency matters, failing to ask about
immigration status when relevant, and using outdated referral lists—occurred at similar rates in
all six organizations. The working group concluded that the root cause was not staff competence but
the absence of a shared baseline of knowledge.

In 2009, the Collaborative’s board approved the creation of a Training Committee with a mandate to
develop a common curriculum. The committee met monthly for one year and produced the first version
of the Case Coordination Training Program manual in 2010. That first edition was 12 hours in
duration and was delivered entirely in person. It covered intake fundamentals, referral management,
and confidentiality requirements.

The first edition was well received, but it also revealed an important limitation: because all
training was delivered in person, staff at smaller organizations often had to wait several months
before a training session was offered in their area. This delay meant that new staff were sometimes
working without having completed the full program. In response, the committee began exploring
options for self-paced learning.

Northeast Legal Aid Collaborative founding year 1998 year. Record status: historical.

**4.3 Transition to Blended Delivery**

In 2014, the Collaborative piloted a hybrid format. The self-paced online modules were introduced
for the foundational content, while the live sessions were reserved for interactive exercises and
case discussions. The pilot involved 24 participants from four member organizations. Feedback from
the pilot indicated that participants appreciated the flexibility of the online modules but
struggled with the transition between online content and live sessions. Some participants reported
that they had forgotten key concepts from the online modules by the time they attended the live
sessions.

The Training Committee addressed this issue by introducing the requirement that participants
complete at least Modules 1 through 4 before attending the first live session. This requirement has
remained in place in subsequent editions and is reflected in the current scheduling guidance
provided in Section 2 of this manual.

**4.4 The 2018 Restructuring**

The most significant revision to the program occurred in 2018. That year, the Collaborative merged
with two additional regional legal aid networks, bringing the total number of member organizations
to eleven. The merger created a need to harmonize not only the training content but also the
terminology used across the organizations. For example, what some organizations called “urgent”
matters were referred to as “priority” matters in others. The 2018 edition of the manual introduced
the standardized intake categories that are still in use today.

## Section 2: Training Schedule and Delivery Methods

### 2.1 Overview of Annual Training Cycle

The Collaborative operates a structured annual training cycle designed to ensure that all case coordinators, intake specialists, and support staff receive consistent, high-quality instruction regardless of their organization's size or location. The cycle is organized around six training sessions per year, with each session focusing on a distinct cluster of competencies. This schedule allows new staff to enter the program at multiple points throughout the year while still completing the full curriculum within a reasonable timeframe.

**Table 2-A: Annual Training Sessions at a Glance**

Sarah Okafor, the Training Director, oversees 6 training sessions per year. Record status: current. This arrangement has been in effect since the 2021 program review and remains current as of the publication of this edition. The Training Director is responsible for coordinating session logistics, approving facilitator assignments, and ensuring that each session meets the learning objectives outlined in the corresponding module.

### 2.2 Scheduling Principles

The annual schedule follows several guiding principles that have been refined over successive editions of this manual:

1. **Geographic rotation.** Live sessions rotate among the four regional hubs: Portland, Manchester, Hartford, and Providence. This rotation ensures that no single member organization bears a disproportionate travel burden.

3. **Timing relative to grant cycles.** Sessions 3 and 5 are scheduled to coincide with common grant reporting periods. This timing allows case coordinators to apply documentation and ethical reasoning skills to their current caseloads.

**Module 3: Intake Procedures**

**Learning Objectives**

After completing this module, participants will be able to:

- List the three stages of the intake process and the purpose of each stage.
- Apply the eligibility screening criteria to determine whether a caller qualifies for services.
- Use the standardized intake form (Form 3-A) to record the required information during the initial call.
- Identify when a case should be flagged for same-day review and when it should be routed to the after-hours line.
- Explain the difference between intake and referral and complete the referral cover sheet (Form 3-C) correctly.

**3.1 Overview of the Intake Process**

Intake is the first point of contact between a potential client and a member organization. The quality of the intake process determines whether the caller receives the right help at the right time, and it sets the tone for the entire case relationship. For many callers, the intake call is their first experience with legal aid, and they may be anxious, confused, or unsure whether they qualify for help. A well-run intake process is efficient, respectful, and thorough.

The intake process has three stages:

1. **Triage:** The caller’s immediate safety and urgency needs are identified.
2. **Eligibility Screening:** The caller’s legal problem and income are reviewed against the program’s eligibility criteria.
3. **Documentation:** The intake information is recorded on Form 3-A and entered into the case management system (CMS).

These stages are described in detail in the sections that follow. The order of the stages is important. Do not skip triage to move directly to eligibility screening. Even if a caller is clearly ineligible based on income, the triage stage may reveal a safety concern that requires immediate action, such as a referral to emergency shelter or law enforcement.

**3.2 Stage One: Triage**

The purpose of triage is to identify any immediate safety or urgency issues before proceeding with the full intake. Triage should take no more than two to three minutes. The following questions are part of the standard triage script (Form 3-B):

- “Are you in a safe place to talk right now?”
- “Is there any immediate danger to you or anyone in your household?”
- “Do you have a court date or hearing within the next five business days?”
- “Are you facing eviction or loss of housing within the next ten days?”

If the caller answers “yes” to any of the triage questions, the intake worker should follow the Urgent Case Protocol described in Section 3.4. Do not proceed with the full eligibility screening until the urgency issue has been addressed.

If the caller answers “no” to all triage questions, proceed to Stage Two.

**3.3 Stage Two: Eligibility Screening**

Eligibility screening is conducted in two parts: legal problem eligibility and income eligibility. Both parts must be satisfied for the caller to receive full services from the member organization. If the caller does not meet one of the parts, the intake worker should complete the Referral Cover Sheet (Form 3-C) and route the caller to the appropriate resource.

**3.3.1 Legal Problem Eligibility**

The following legal problem types are within the scope of services for the current grant year:

- Eviction defense and housing habitability
- Family law matters involving domestic violence or child custody
- Consumer debt collection defense
- Public benefits denials and terminations
- Guardianship of minors
- Employment discrimination

**3.3.2 Income Eligibility**

Income eligibility is determined using the current federal poverty guidelines, adjusted for
household size. The income limit for full services is set at 125% of the federal poverty level
(FPL), unless a specific grant or contract allows a higher limit. A chart listing the current
income limits by household size is posted at each intake station and is also available as Form

The following sources of income must be counted when determining eligibility:

- Wages, salaries, tips, and commissions
- Self-employment income (net)
- Unemployment compensation
- Workers’ compensation
- Social Security benefits, including retirement, disability, and survivor benefits
- Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
- Veterans’ benefits
- Pensions and retirement accounts
- Interest and dividends
- Rental income
- Child support and alimony received
- Regular contributions from household members or others

In-kind benefits such as SNAP (food stamps), Medicaid, or housing vouchers are not counted as
income for eligibility purposes. If a caller’s income is close to the limit, the intake worker
should calculate the annualized amount using the instructions on Form 3-D. When income
information is unclear or incomplete, the intake worker should ask the caller to provide
documentation before making a final determination. A caller who refuses to provide income
documentation may be offered limited advice or a referral, but full representation cannot be
approved without verification.

**3.3.3 Household Definition**

For income eligibility purposes, a household includes all individuals who live together and share
income and expenses, regardless of legal or marital status. The income of all household members
over the age of 18 is counted, except for the following:

- Income of a minor child, unless it is used for household expenses
- Income of a live-in attendant or caregiver
- Income of a roomer or boarder who is not part of the family unit
- Student financial aid used for tuition and educational expenses

If a caller is seeking assistance for a matter that affects only one household member, such as a
guardianship of a minor, the income of that minor is not counted. The intake worker should use
the household composition worksheet on Form 3-E to record the information.

**3.4 Urgent Case Protocol**

When a caller answers “yes” to any triage question, the intake worker must follow the Urgent Case
Protocol. The purpose of this protocol is to stabilize the immediate crisis while beginning the
eligibility screening. The intake worker should:

1.  Ask the caller for the best phone number and a safe time to call back.
2.  Determine whether the caller needs immediate referral to emergency services, such as police,
    domestic violence shelter, or adult protective services. If so, make the referral before
    proceeding with any other questions.
3.  If the issue involves a court hearing, document the court date, time, courthouse, and case
    number on the Urgent Case Log (Form 3-F).
4.  Notify the supervising attorney or the designated urgent case coordinator by email or phone
    within one hour of the call.
5.  Complete the full eligibility screening within one business day, unless the urgency issue
    requires immediate action sooner.

Urgent cases are assigned a priority level of P1. The supervising attorney must review the case
file within two hours of the initial call to determine whether emergency advocacy is needed, such
as a motion for a temporary restraining order or an emergency eviction defense.

**Module 4: Communication, Case Handoffs, and Documentation Standards**

**Learning Objectives**

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

1.  Use the two-zone communication model for client and partner organization contact.
2.  Prepare a complete case handoff package using the standardized transfer checklist.
3.  Apply the documentation standards for case notes, including the DAP format.
4.  Identify and correct common documentation errors through the quality review process.
5.  Respond to a partner organization’s request for case information in accordance with confidentiality requirements.

**4.1 The Two-Zone Communication Model**

Effective case coordination depends on clear, consistent communication between member organizations. NELAC uses a two-zone model to help staff distinguish between routine updates and time-sensitive alerts. The model is simple: every message you send about a case falls into one of two zones, and each zone has its own expectations for timeliness and format.

**Zone 1: Routine Communication**

Zone 1 covers information that is important but does not require immediate action. Examples include:

- Confirming receipt of a referral
- Sending a completed eligibility screening
- Updating a case log after a scheduled appointment
- Sharing general program information with a partner

Zone 1 messages must be sent within two business days of the event they document. They may be sent by email, through the shared case management portal, or by fax if the receiving organization has indicated a preference for fax. When using email, include the case number in the subject line and copy the designated case coordinator at the receiving organization.

**Zone 2: Urgent Communication**

Zone 2 covers situations where a delay could harm the client or jeopardize a legal deadline. Examples include:

- A court hearing scheduled within five business days
- An eviction notice with a hearing date
- A request from a partner organization for immediate assistance with a client in crisis
- A change in a client’s contact information when a court filing is pending

Zone 2 messages must be sent within four hours of learning of the situation. If the receiving organization does not respond within two hours, the sender must follow up by phone. Zone 2 messages should be sent by phone and email, and the case coordinator should confirm receipt in writing.

**Table 4-A: Communication Zones at a Glance**

| Zone | Examples | Time to Send | Method | Follow-Up |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Zone 1 | Routine updates, confirmations | Within 2 business days | Email, portal, fax | None required |
| Zone 2 | Court deadlines, crises | Within 4 hours | Phone and email | Phone call if no response in 2 hours |

**4.2 Case Handoffs and the Transfer Checklist**

A case handoff occurs when responsibility for a case moves from one staff member to another, either within your organization or to a partner organization. Handoffs are high-risk moments for losing information, missing deadlines, or confusing the client. To reduce this risk, every handoff must be documented using the Case Transfer Checklist (Form 4-A).

**When to Use the Transfer Checklist**

Use Form 4-A in the following situations:

- Assigning a new case to an attorney or advocate
- Transferring a case from one NELAC member organization to another
- Closing a case and referring the client to a different service provider
- Covering a colleague’s caseload during an absence of more than three business days

**Module 5: Ethics, Confidentiality, and Conflict of Interest**

**5.1 Learning Objectives**

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

- Identify the ethical obligations that apply to case coordination under the NELAC Standards of Practice
- Apply the confidentiality rules to routine, urgent, and handoff communications
- Recognize a conflict of interest before it compromises a case
- Use the Conflict of Interest Disclosure Form (Form 5-A) correctly
- Respond appropriately when a client’s confidentiality must be breached under law or court order

**5.2 The Ethical Framework for Case Coordination**

Case coordination sits at the intersection of legal representation, social services, and information sharing. Because coordinators handle sensitive client information across organizations, ethical rules apply even when the coordinator is not the client’s attorney of record. The NELAC Standards of Practice incorporate the ethical rules of each jurisdiction where a member organization operates, and where those rules conflict, the stricter standard applies.

Three principles anchor all case coordination work:

1. **Client-centeredness.** The client’s interests, not the interests of the referring or receiving organization, drive every decision.
2. **Least-disclosure.** Share only the minimum information necessary to accomplish the coordination task.
3. **Accountability.** Every disclosure, refusal, and judgment call must be documented so that another coordinator can review the decision later.

**5.3 Confidentiality: What Is Protected**

Confidential information includes any information relating to the representation of a client, regardless of its source. This includes:

- The client’s name and contact information
- The fact that a client is seeking or receiving services
- Case facts, including those the client has shared orally or in writing
- Legal strategy, even if not yet executed
- Payment information, including fee arrangements and grant eligibility
- Records from other agencies that have been shared with your organization

The duty of confidentiality survives the end of representation. It also survives the end of employment. A coordinator who leaves a NELAC member organization remains bound by the confidentiality rules for any case they worked on.

**5.4 When Confidential Information May Be Disclosed**

The general rule is: no disclosure without client consent. Exceptions are narrow and must be documented.

**5.4.1 Client Consent**

Consent must be informed, in writing, and specific to the disclosure. A general consent to “share my information with partner agencies” is not sufficient for a specific referral or handoff. The consent must identify:

- The information to be shared
- The recipient or class of recipients
- The purpose of the disclosure
- The time period for which the consent is valid

Use Form 5-B (Client Consent for Disclosure of Information) for all consents. A copy must be placed in the case file and forwarded with any disclosed information.

**5.4.2 Implied Consent for Coordination**

When a client has asked your organization to coordinate with another entity, consent to share the information necessary to complete that coordination is implied. For example, if a client asks you to help them apply for emergency rental assistance, you may share the income and household information needed to complete the application. You may not share unrelated case facts, such as a pending criminal matter, without separate consent.

documents.title: NELAC Policy on Case Triage
documents.content:
This policy applies to all staff, volunteers, interns, and contractors who perform intake, screening, or case-eligibility functions at any NELAC member organization. It covers requests for assistance received by telephone, in person, by mail, through web portals, or by referral from partner agencies. The policy does not apply to requests for legal information that do not involve an assessment of eligibility or a request for representation, nor does it apply to matters already accepted for representation.

**3. Definitions**

For purposes of this policy:

- **Applicant:** An individual or household seeking legal assistance from a member organization.
- **Case Triage:** The process of assessing an applicant's legal problem to determine urgency, eligibility, and appropriate service path.
- **Emergency Matter:** A matter in which there is an imminent court hearing, deadline, or risk of irreparable harm to the applicant's person, liberty, housing, or subsistence.
- **Priority 1 (P1):** Matters that require action within one business day due to an imminent deadline or emergency circumstance.
- **Priority 2 (P2):** Matters that require action within five business days, typically involving a pending deadline or significant adverse consequence if delayed.
- **Priority 3 (P3):** Matters that are not time-sensitive and can be addressed through routine scheduling or referral.
- **Service Path:** The assigned route for handling a matter, including full representation, brief service, advice and referral, self-help materials, or referral to a partner agency.
- **Conflict Check:** A review of existing and former client records to determine whether representation of an applicant would create a conflict of interest under applicable rules of professional conduct.

**4. Eligibility Criteria**

Member organizations shall determine eligibility for services using the following baseline criteria, subject to any additional requirements imposed by funding sources or specific grant terms:

The Legal Aid Intake Manual's last revision date is 2024-08-15. Record status: historical.

- **Income:** Applicants whose household income does not exceed 200% of the federal poverty guidelines shall be presumed eligible. Applicants above this threshold may be considered for services on a case-by-case basis if they demonstrate significant financial hardship, such as high medical expenses, recent unemployment, or a pending foreclosure or eviction.
- **Assets:** Liquid assets exceeding $10,000, excluding retirement accounts and the applicant's primary residence, shall ordinarily make an applicant ineligible unless the matter involves a threat to the applicant's housing or safety.
- **Residency or Service Area:** Applicants must reside in or have a legal matter arising within the service area of the member organization, except where a referral from another legal aid program or a court appointment requires otherwise.
- **Merit:** The matter must present a viable legal claim or defense. Matters that are frivolous, lacking in factual basis, or outside the organization's practice areas may be declined.

Eligibility determinations shall be documented in the intake record, including the basis for any exception to the baseline criteria. When an applicant is found ineligible, the intake worker shall provide information about alternative resources, including bar association referral services, self-help centers, and other community-based organizations, to the extent such information is available.

**5. Priority Categories**

All matters shall be assigned a priority category at the time of intake. The assigning worker shall consider the immediacy of any deadline, the severity of the consequences of inaction, and the applicant's vulnerability, including age, disability, language access needs, or risk of homelessness.

**NELAC Policy on Case Triage**
Effective January 1, 2024
Reviewed Annually

---

**5. Priority Categories (continued)**

Priority categories shall be assigned according to the following tiers, which are intended to guide, not replace, the professional judgment of the intake worker and supervising attorney. When a matter falls squarely within more than one tier, the higher priority shall apply.

- **Priority 1 (P1):** Matters involving an imminent court deadline, hearing, or filing date within the next seven (7) calendar days; matters where the applicant faces loss of housing, including eviction proceedings or foreclosure sales scheduled within the next thirty (30) days; matters involving the immediate physical safety of the applicant or a household member, including protection order applications; and matters where government benefits that are the applicant's sole source of income have been terminated or are scheduled for termination within the next fourteen (14) days.
- **Priority 2 (P2):** Matters involving a court deadline or filing date within the next eight (8) to thirty (30) days; matters where the applicant faces a substantial risk of loss of housing, including pending lease terminations or mortgage default notices; matters involving denial, reduction, or overpayment of government benefits where an appeal deadline is within the next thirty (30) days; and matters involving a significant consumer or financial issue that threatens the applicant's basic necessities, such as utility shut-off, wage garnishment, or vehicle repossession.
- **Priority 3 (P3):** Matters involving a court deadline or filing date more than thirty (30) days out; matters involving family law issues, including divorce, custody, and child support, where no emergency custody or safety issue is present; matters involving housing conditions, including repair and habitability disputes; and matters involving consumer debt collection where no immediate garnishment or levy is scheduled.
- **Priority 4 (P4):** All other matters that meet eligibility criteria but do not present an immediate deadline or threat to basic necessities. These matters may be placed on a waiting list, referred to a pro bono panel, or scheduled for a clinic or advice session, as resources permit.

The intake worker shall document the assigned priority category and the specific facts supporting that assignment in the intake record. If a matter is later reclassified to a different priority category, the reclassification shall be noted in the case file, including the date and the name of the person authorizing the change.

**6. Appeals of Priority or Eligibility Determinations**

An applicant who disagrees with an eligibility or priority determination may request review. The following procedures shall apply:

Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent a member organization from providing immediate assistance to an applicant pending the outcome of an appeal where the matter involves an imminent deadline or a threat to the applicant's safety.

**7. Documentation and Recordkeeping**

Member organizations shall maintain accurate and complete records for all matters, including matters that are declined, referred, or placed on a waiting list. At a minimum, the following documentation shall be retained:

- The completed intake form, including all eligibility and priority determinations and the basis for any exceptions.
- Correspondence with the applicant, including notices of determination and appeal decisions.
- A case log or case management system entry reflecting all significant case activities, including the date of the activity, the person performing the activity, and a brief description.
- Copies of all pleadings, correspondence, and other legal documents prepared or received in connection with the matter.
- Records of any referrals made to other resources, including the name of the referral source and the date of the referral.
